verdicts.trueWording: gothic atmosphere is clearly set through the daunting presence of the statue
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'rather than by naming the mood' - Hewitt draws no such contrast
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (Meghan Hewitt, 15 Dec 2024 byline confirmed). Quote is verbatim: 'The gothic atmosphere is clearly set through the daunting presence of the statue, as well as the skeletal remains lurking in the corners of the room.' The room is the Strahd shrine in the Death House module of Curse of Strahd, and the module description she quotes is all physical objects (moldy skeletons, rusty shackles, painted wooden statue). But Hewitt never contrasts object-description with mood-naming; that contrastive limb is the claimant's inference, not her argument.

verdicts.trueWording: Strahd's suggested actions and descriptions do not change from one text to the other
verdicts.note: Raw page. Full sentence: 'Despite this, Strahd's suggested actions and descriptions do not change from one text to the other to reflect this change in alignment, directly contradicting the role of alignment in D&D.' The alignment change (Chaotic Evil in Ravenloft to Lawful Evil in Curse of Strahd) is stated two sentences earlier. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: this style of adventure has gradually fallen out of style in favor of fifth edition's style of heroism and clarity in description
verdicts.note: Raw page (Mark Hines, 19 Mar 2023 byline confirmed). Preceding sentence: 'Many of the tricks and traps in Gygax's original adventure are indiscernible, devious, fatal, and intentionally counterintuitive.' The contrast the claim describes is explicit and adjacent. Quote verbatim within 'fifth edition's style of heroism and clarity in description and execution of narrative.'

verdicts.trueWording: Economics play a large role in the events described
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'dominate' - Peterson says only that economics 'play a large role'
verdicts.note: Raw page. Quote verbatim, and the 1971 dating is on the page ('it seems safe to accept 1071 as 1971 ... late in the fall of that year'). But Peterson does not claim economics dominate: the same post gives comparable weight to the wargame component ('several thousand enemy troops') and to fantastic elements (dragons, 'evil creatures overrunning the region'). 'Dominate' overstates 'play a large role'.

verdicts.trueWording: The Wizard pays restitution for damages caused by his dragon's mischievous offspring
verdicts.note: Raw page. All three listed items are on the page in one paragraph: 'Inspector General John of Snyder comes to collect taxes.' / 'The Wizard pays restitution for damages caused by his dragon's mischievous offspring.' / 'Baron Jenkins has "all but ruined the tavern," and that too sounds like an expensive error on his part.' Quote is an exact substring. Peterson lists a fourth money item too (gypsy fortune telling), which does not contradict the claim's civic-and-financial characterisation.

verdicts.trueWording: does not tell us a great deal about the system of Blackmoor, but it does give significant insight into the setting and the state of the campaign
verdicts.note: Raw page. Both limbs are in one sentence about the Blackmoor Gazette and Rumormonger. 'Earliest' is supported: the post is on issue #1 and refers forward to 'the next issue of the BMG&R (which seems to date from the following year).'

verdicts.trueWording: The earliest explicit use I've found was that of Pieter Roos ... The Wild Hunt #15 (1977)
verdicts.note: Raw page. Full sentence: 'The earliest explicit use I've found was that of Pieter Roos, as shown in this excerpt above from The Wild Hunt #15 (1977), where he identifies it as the overall goal of playing RPGs.' Subject of the paragraph is the term 'immersion'. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Carr clearly connects 'playing your character's role' with his call to 'immerse yourself in the game setting'
verdicts.note: Raw page. The exhibit immediately preceding that sentence is 'The tips for players in his module In Search of the Unknown (B1)' (the excerpt image filename is 1979-b1-carr-tips.jpg), with Boot Hill named as 'similar language.' Quote verbatim. Minor ambiguity only: Peterson attributes the connection to Carr generally rather than naming B1 in that sentence, but B1's player tips are the exhibit he has just presented.

verdicts.trueWording: the location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible
verdicts.note: Raw page (Justin Alexander, The Alexandrian, May 19th, 2014, confirmed on page). Third sentence of the article: 'Which is why I find it fairly surprising that the location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The description of the key, however, was instructional rather than practical
verdicts.note: Raw page, 'A Brief History of the Key' section: 'In 1974, the original edition of D&D included a "Sample Map" keyed with both numbers and letters. The description of the key, however, was instructional rather than practical.' Quote verbatim; the 1974 sample-map limb is the immediately preceding sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: the Gygax 'wall of text' key which would become a staple at TSR for the better part of a decade
verdicts.note: Raw page, same section, on The Lost Caverns of Tsojconth. Quote verbatim. 'Undivided' is a fair gloss: Alexander's own contrast is with Blake's 'DM Only' split and with B1, which 'effectively created the idea of separating the key into distinct sections.' The claim's definite article ('the TSR staple' for 'a staple') is a wording shift, not an added limb.

verdicts.trueWording: he introduced that organization by including a 'DM Only' section in each key entry ... effectively accomplishing the same thing on a structural level
verdicts.note: Raw page. All limbs present: Bob Blake, Judges Guild, Gen Con IX Dungeons in the 1976 paragraph; the split entry; and 'Although not technically boxed text, this format was effectively accomplishing the same thing on a structural level.' Reinforced later by 'Like Blake's "DM Only" section from earlier in the decade, the boxed text clearly delineated...'

verdicts.trueWording: the text was not yet boxed, instead appearing between quotation marks ... But in 1980, TSR reissued the module
verdicts.note: Raw page, 'The Era of Boxed Text'. Both limbs: original Lost Tamoachan text 'not yet boxed, instead appearing between quotation marks', then 'But in 1980, TSR reissued the module as C1 The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan, placing the prewritten descriptions in a box for the first time.'

verdicts.trueWording: the boxed text clearly delineated the elements ... that should be immediately shared with any PC entering the area
verdicts.note: Raw page, same section. Quote verbatim. Alexander does add that boxed text's role 'would be expanded' later to any read-aloud text, but the definitional limb the claim states is exactly his.

verdicts.trueWording: if they did appear then they appeared in that order and no other
verdicts.note: Raw page, 'Adventure Formatting Guides': 3rd Edition's new 'standard format', 'First appearing in The Sunless Citadel', with 'a specific set of bold-faced sections' (Traps, Creatures, Tactics, Development, Treasure). Note the page's qualifier, which the claim does not contradict: 'Not all of these appeared in every location, but if they did appear then they appeared in that order and no other.'
